stem:
Are the two groups cis or trans? Is this the most stable conformation? If it is not, draw the one that is.
[[chair:1u:CH(CH3)2,2u:Cl|A]]

steps.h: Isopropyl on C1 is on a vertical bond: axial. Cl on C2 points outward, roughly parallel to the ring bonds one bond away: equatorial.

Every ring carbon has one bond that points more up and one that points more down. Axial bonds alternate up, down, up around the ring. The axial isopropyl points straight up. At C2 the axial bond points down, so the equatorial bond is the up one: Cl is up.

ask.q: At C2 the axial bond points down. Is the equatorial bond there the up one or the down one?
ask.a: The up one. The two bonds on a ring carbon always point to opposite faces.

steps.h: Both groups are up: same face, so cis. On neighbouring carbons (1,2): one axial and one equatorial is cis. Two equatorial, or two axial, is trans.

ask.q: Are the two groups on the same face or on opposite faces?

steps.h: One group must be axial in either chair, so the question is which. Axial isopropyl costs 2.61 kcal/mol (Table 5.3). Axial Cl would cost about 0.53 kcal/mol (a literature value: the lecture table lists only alkyl groups). The larger group, isopropyl, is axial here. This chair is not the most stable one.

ask.q: Which of the two groups costs more when it is axial?
ask.a: Isopropyl. It is the one that should be equatorial.

steps.h:
Flip the ring: every axial group becomes equatorial and every equatorial group becomes axial. Up stays up and down stays down, so the molecule is still cis.
[[chair:1u:CH(CH3)2,2u:Cl|B]]

solution.answer: cis; no. The most stable chair is the ring flip: isopropyl equatorial, Cl axial.
solution.rule: 1,2: axial and equatorial is cis; equatorial and equatorial (or axial and axial) is trans. Larger group equatorial.

ask.a: Make both axial, which costs energy. So the drawn chair is the better one.
